div1.head: Interview with Dora Janet Au Mahoney [3/3/2003]

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Today is Monday, March 3, 2003. This is the beginning of an interview with Dora Janet Au Mahoney at the Erlanger Health Plus Office, 975 East Third Street, Chattanooga, Tennessee. Ms. Mahoney was born on November 7, 1921, and is now 81 years old. My name is Michael Willie, and I will conduct this interview. Ms. Mahoney, could you state for the recording your name and its spelling, please.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Dora Janet Au Mahoney, A-U M-A-H-O-N-E-Y.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. Where were you born, Ms. Mahoney?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Rossville, Georgia, Walker County.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Explain where that is in Georgia.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Oh, it's two miles -- Rossville city has a boundary of Chattanooga and Rossville run together. We could walk across the street with one foot in Tennessee and one in Georgia.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right. So we're right at the north part of Georgia and the Tennessee line. Tell me about your family. Do you have any brothers or sisters?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: I had two sisters and two brothers.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: What were their ages relative to yours?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: To mine?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Yeah. How much older or younger were they?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Older. My oldest sister was 16 and a high school graduate when I was born.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: My older brother was 15; the next sister was 13. Then there was a skip for several years; a brother 17 months older than I, and he was born in 1920 and me in '21.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And what did your parents do? What did your dad do for a living in Rossville?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Farmer.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. And at that time -- were you saying that your sister had -- she was a high school graduate and had moved out by the time you were born?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: No. She was at home. She took care of the two little ones. Mom and daddy ran a dairy and she took care of us. In fact, I called her Mamalene.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Now, so you're born in Rossville, Georgia. Were you raised there, too? Did you spend your formative years all there in Rossville --

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- or did you move at any time?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: No. I graduated from high school from Rossville, went in first grade in the same building I graduated. And we had only 11 years in that time, so I graduated when I was 16.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And were you spending any time -- did you work at all with your parents at the dairy?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: No. Daddy's health failed, and they had to give it up.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: But I did help him in the garden and like walking for acres of dropping corn, a grain of corn at every step to plant the corn. And we always had cows. We helped him at the barn feeding the animals and just home chores.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. All right. Now, as you graduated from high school, coming out of high school -- number one, let's talk about entertainment. What would typically -- what would be your typical weekend when you were in high school? What did you do for entertainment?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Well, occasionally we would have a class party. For instance, we had one at my house and a lot of the football boys came and we played football -- I mean fruit basket turnover.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: What's fruit basket turnover?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: That's where you would jump up and move to another chair, but there's always one chair less and you couldn't find a seat. So about three football players landed on our couch, and the metal springs in there went ping, ping and they just shot up through the couch. And in the winter we would go somewhere and make taffy, pull the taffy in cold weather out on the porch. Went to all the basketball games and football games, all the house -- school plays. We were active in the youth activities at our church, center youth choir. And we did come into Chattanooga very often. We were 10 miles out of Chattanooga, and it was a special trip to come into town to shop.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Now, let's talk about your expectations when you come out of high school. Now, at that time are you thinking when you get out of high school that you're going to get married or are you thinking you're going to go to college or get a job or what is your expectation coming out of high school?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: I wanted to go to college, but we couldn't afford that and being 16 I had to wait until I was 18 to get a Social Security card to do any public work. So I took a correspondence course of some kind from a company in Chicago. It was more than I could comprehend. And then I would think some day I'll marry, but I don't know who and right then I -- there's no boy or man alive that I wanted to cook for.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Now, so you stopped the correspondence course; is that it?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Yes, I did, finally. I took piano lessons.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: And sang in a choir. WILIE: Okay. And you're still at home, right?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Yeah, yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Living at home. And you're basically just -- I mean life is good at this time would you say?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Oh, yes, very good.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Did you have a steady boyfriend?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: No, no. We just kind of ran around with a group.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Now, let's work up until you turn 20, okay.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Going where?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Until you turn 20.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Now, when you're 20 years old, where are you living? Are you still at home?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And do you remember the day Pearl Harbor was bombed?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Oh, definitely. We were having lunch and the radio was on and that news came on, and I began to worry right then because I knew my brother would have to go to war.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And was he -- was he drafted or did he join?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Which one? Was he drafted or did he join?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: He was -- he was drafted, I believe, and had a business course education, and he was put in the medical field for some reason and got into hospital administration.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Does this influence you at all?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Include me?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Does this influence you at all?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Oh, no. No, it didn't.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Now, at that time when you're 20 years old and the war breaks out, at this time do you have a steady boyfriend or anything?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: No. Everybody went into service, you know. It was just a bunch of girls left by themselves.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: I remember our minister had a pageant or play, and he did it just so that we would have something to do because we didn't have any boyfriends. Now, when I was 20 I went to work at the TNT plant. I went into training at Erlanger for my clinical laboratory work at age 19.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Didn't know that. Okay. So talking about the clinical lab work then, what basically is that? Is that like a nursing school or is that --

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Erlanger is a teaching school. So they had a school for many different occupations or auxiliary type of work assisting a doctor or the medical facilities. Do you want me to tell you something about -- I said it's a teaching school. Our tuition was free. They furnish meals and uniform laundry. And we bought our textbooks. And we could not live on campus. So, again, I still stayed at home and commuted to the hospital.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Now, at this time are you going to school for a specific skill or a trade or do you get to choose that or how does that work when you come in?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: I chose to do that. I was taking a business course and working part-time at a five- and ten-cent store for 15 cents an hour, and I knew there was something better than that. I was taking this business course and I met my friend at the bus stop downtown. She was having her half day off. And she described to me what she was doing at the hospital laboratory. And in the clinical lab you run tests on all body fluids. And she had her textbook and showed me things I would see through the microscope and it fascinated me. So she said we have an opening. Why don't you go talk to them. So I went and had an interview with Dr. Dietrich. He was over radiology and the lab. And I said, is there any special insurance that I have to take out to work here? And he just laughed. He said, no. We just wash our hands with Palmolive soap. And they took a new student every six weeks and you were called a lily. You wore your street clothes until they decided you were someone that could go through the course and then you went to your uniforms. But as you went out in your street clothes with someone in a uniform to observe what they were doing and collecting the blood specimens, people would call you a lily, a new lily. And we worked until the work was done. There was an evening shift came in, but day work that came in late that we had to collect, that had to be finished before we went home. And sometimes we worked from eight to nine p.m. There was nothing unusual to stay that long.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right. Now, is this -- you say this is -- basically it's a teaching school. So is this like -- how long does the course last?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: It was 13 months.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Thirteen months.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: And then they had radiology for another year and you could take both courses or one, either one you chose. I chose to take two. But I just got started in radiology and had some anatomy, terminology, the instructions of the darkroom, developing the films. And I had applied at the TNT plant. One of my favorite supervisors had applied and was accepted and was going to be the lab supervisor up there. And she said, there will be openings for other people in the lab. So I sent in an application and had not heard from them. And I went on into this introduction to radiology when I got a telephone call. And the plant -- Hercules plant manager called and asked if I could come to work that day. And I told him, yes, sir, but I don't have transportation to get out there. And he said, oh, we will send a government car to pick you up and meet us at the hospital entrance and there will be someone there to pick you up. So they drove me up to the plant. And you cross the railroad tracks and into the main entrance, which was under guard, and took me to the administration building on the right of the main drive. And I was -- answered a lot of questions and photographed and took my fingerprints. Then they took me in the car on down the road to the field hospital. It had been a cafeteria and the hospital were in a median strip, wide strip between two roads parallel. So there the hospital was accessible on either side. There were doors opening on each road. And we had two ambulances and no air-conditioning, no fans, no intercom, no dictaphones for the doctors, one electric cooler, water fountain, several rooms, boards with six beds, four beds, two single rooms with a single bed; the medical director's office. There's some type of storage in one area. This was just a one-story long building. And the cafeteria and the hospital were pretty far apart. All buildings were built with spaces between so that if one caught on fire, they hoped another one wouldn't be caught. And the treatment room, emergency room was a combination, a large room with double doors and then outside were the ambulances, a waiting room; the medical director's office. That was a single board or single bed in the next room. And then we came to the great large room, one for the lab and next to it was a doctor's office and another doctor's office. And then on down at the end of the building you were to the file room and a small waiting room. Coming back the other side you came to a small room for the lab, another small room for the lab and then the other room that had the single bed, another doctor's office and then a good-sized women's lounge and you're back to the -- at that time you're back to the treatment center. On the other side, the far end of the treatment center, we had two x-ray rooms and a darkroom for developing.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Now, had you taken the radiology course?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: I just had that introduction.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: But now my supervisor, Elizabeth Smith, had a degree, had taught school, changed her occupation and attended Gradwall (ph) school for two years, and that was laboratory technology and radiology. So she accepted a job at Erlanger, 12 hours a night, five nights a week, for 100 dollars a month. And then she was finally put on the day shift. And there's where we had a supervisor in each lab for our training. And it was on-the-job training. So she told me about this -- these openings that would be at the TNT plant. She had been accepted but had to work two week's notice. So when they called me, I went out there alone. And I walked into this room that was such a clutter and these big baseboard boxes that had been opened. Everything that had been ordered and came through shipping had to be opened and inspected. So these things were sitting everywhere, on counters and the floor, and they evidently thought our manuals were packing. They threw the manuals away. And the reason they called me that day, they had lined up five or six people to come through for their laboratory work and get their physical to get ready to put them on a job. And I looked around for the equipment I needed and finally found what I thought was enough that I could do blood counts and couldn't find any containers for the urinalysis. So I went down to the medical director and was so happy to see him, because he happened to be a doctor who had interned and done a residence program at Erlanger. And so we knew each other. He sent someone to the cafeteria down the street to bring milk bottles back for the urine specimen collections. And I thought -- we had been taught to make up -- do alternate ways of performing the test. So there's -- one thing was the hemoglobin was very important, but I knew an alternate method, a reagent to use. And I couldn't find the reagent for what I really needed. So I made this alternate and drew up a red cell count and a white cell count, made my blood smear. And the blood for the white cells should have been a combination that the red cells would have ruptured, the iron would appear as a brown color and I could have read that with a color comparison, but it didn't work that way. Everything was as clear as water. The white cells were there and the red cells were destroyed, so I couldn't read a hemoglobin. And I had to call the plant director now and tell him what a mistake I had made. He was very nice about it. And he said, well, you get everything you need all in order and together, and we will have them come back tomorrow for a repeat. He was very nice and, oh, I was so relieved. And from then on I was working there every day for 40 months.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Now, let's talk about what was going on at the plant. Talk about everything that was going on. What was the job at the plant basically?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: The job where?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: What was going on at the plant? What were they producing?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: At the plant?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: It was under construction, but they were -- by Stone and Webster, but they were also beginning to do the physicals for Hercules employees; the people who would be in production and all of the people that had anything to do with the TNT.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Stone and Webster was the contractor for all of the buildings.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right. But that's what I'm trying to get out is the TNT. They were there to produce TNT, right?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Yes, yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And then it says something about acid, too.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Acid -- TNT was made with acid. It involved nitric acid and toluene and then sulfuric acid was involved to withdraw water from these three agents. And the compound that was made had to be dried. But if it got too hot, it would catch on fire and be combustionable. So water, cold water was run through coils in these lines to keep the TNT cool so it wouldn't explode -- or not explode, but to catch on fire. And the sulfuric fumes were awful, just terrible. They didn't have filters for all of this exhaust that was coming out and it also created fog. In the mornings the fog would be so dense it might be 11 o'clock before you could see clear sun and the acid was so strong your teeth were on edge. Now, that was out of the restricted area. And the production people were in a restricted area, another gate to go through, and they were working right with that acid. The first aid fellas had watched these people closely to see that no one was overcome by the fumes. And the critical point was where the acids were mixed together. Our plant had the largest acid plant in the world. And I don't know how much TNT was produced, but as it came off the lines it was placed in containers. A truck picked up the containers and took those to the shipping dock to be loaded on freight cars or in bunkers. They had 200 bunkers for storage, and they were down in the ground and looked like they had been soldered over. To look over it was a pretty green filled with humps all around. And of course there were no planes flying over. Aircraft was restricted to stay from there. And they had -- there were two main railroads running across at the front entrance, main lines running every day. But our freight cars came in on a spare track of 20 miles, which was laid after they began getting everything in preparedness. That track ran around to the shipping and receiving dock. So the cartons of TNT were put down there and then put into freight cars. Now, I rode with a group of people, and one of them was a woman who worked for the railroad company. I never did understand her job, except it was to climb up on the top of every freight car and write down some information that she looked for up there. And that was tiring for her. On her way home she would be so tired. And that was a lot of cars to climb on. That's all she did every day.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Now, what were you doing -- well, let's see. You were conducting the physicals first as the people come in.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: As they came in, we received like a requisition or a paper with their name. And we were set up to do venous punctures and from that we tested for syphilis. And we pricked their finger for the complete blood count and gave them the urine specimen to be collected; the bottles to collect that. And we did a special -- no, not then. We helped the nurses do eye exams, take temperatures. We had one maid who helped with our glassware. And we washed a lot of our glassware, dried it in an oven. And anything that the doctor wanted to order, we were capable of doing everything, even to cross matching blood. But we never had to do that, because anything serious was sent the patient by our ambulances to Erlanger, which was the only hospital, the largest hospital in Chattanooga. And it was a city-county hospital. So our stopover at our hospital was mainly for the minor treatment. And I had to x-ray things that -- for Hercules to have proof of and for their records. The films that I made were sent on to Erlanger with the patient on an ambulance. For instance, a patient came in. A package had fallen off of a shelf, big heavy thing, and hit her arm. She had a compound fracture. And I had to x-ray that and then get my film out and send it on with her to the hospital.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Occasionally somebody might be put to bed for a while during the day. We did not keep anybody overnight if they came in sick. And our physicals for Africans, those were tremendous. They just came and waited their turn. And at one time I went to the door. I had the name on the paper. I went to the door and I called for Mr. Shelsinger. Nobody got up. And I said Mr. Shelsinger. And the man said are you calling Schlessinger? And so we did make mistakes in name pronunciation. Some of them fainted, of course.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Hold on one second. [Tape is changed.]

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. So how long does the construction actually last? How long does it take before the plant is --

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: The construction?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: How long does it take before the plant is up and running?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: They came to Chattanooga on June 6, 1940.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: And did I tell you about the first office?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Okay. Stone and Webster was -- had their office in a little house outside the main area and across the street was another little house where they had a nurse, a first aid man, and an old hearse for the ambulance. These were located right near the landmark up there called Hunley Store, a country store that sold everything: Horse collars, groceries, post office located in there, spool of thread, anything you needed, material for sewing. It was a quaint little store. And this was all outside the main boundary for the site. The entire place was fenced in with metal fencing. It had an area which is the area we worked in was the outer area and then you went to the gate that was entering the restricted area, and that is where production took place. And then there was another area that surround -- a road that surrounded the bunkers, and they were patrolled continuously. And then the big acid house, a chemical lab, a laboratory for chemicals. And we were doing -- oh, there's another word for the physical -- I mean the body fluids. A general term for that. But they were absolutely different type labs. And then the reservoirs, huge water reservoirs, a water filtration plant and treatment plant. There was also a fire department near the restriction -- inside the restricted area near the gate.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Was this -- I mean where were you -- were you still living at home when you were working?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Yes, I was. I lived 12 miles from the plant. And I'll tell you about our transportation; is that all right?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Because of swing shifts they -- and tires were hard to get. Most people had A stickers. But if they carried passengers to war work areas, they got a B sticker. And the men were willing to drive anywhere to pick you up, miles and miles. There were people that lived on Meade (ph) down in the valley and further down in smaller towns that came by my house and picked me up. Many of them went out of their way. They could have gone a shorter route to Tanner. The site was located at Tanner, Tennessee, on the edge of Chattanooga. And because of swing shifts they were always changing the driver -- I mean your work --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Schedule.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Um-hum. And you put your name on and telephone number on a bulletin board. If you didn't have a ride, you would soon -- somebody would call you. I never had any fear about how I was going to get back and forth. I never worried one minute of how I was going to go to work the next day. Did I tell you I was never late or missed a day? And most cars had five passengers plus the driver.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: They were interesting. The people working in personnel as well as in production were in these groups. They never did say much about their job or if there was an accident that took place. I didn't hear of any real bad accidents. They never -- so as far as I knew, they didn't have any real big fires. The first aid man, D. Coleman, switched over from Stone and Webster after they had done most of their construction work. He changed over to work for Hercules. And there were several young first aid men located in the -- working out of the hospital but located in the restriction area. And he told me at one time fire broke out in three freight cars. And at that time they really didn't know what the -- what would happen -- I mean what was being exposed in the air. So they excavate -- not excavated. They -- I need that word.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: I don't know what you're talking about.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Moving people out.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Oh --

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: What's the word, Carolyn?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: I know what you're talking about. They evacuated?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Well, they moved them away from the site there around in the area that we passed going into the place. And one reason that that site was selected, it was not inhabited very well. There were two houses that had to be destroyed, and I knew the names of one of the families. They had 50 acres and their son worked in the water treatment area until he was called to service. I thought that was interesting. And in excavating and setting the terrain like it needed to be, they dug out, oh, hundreds of yards of dirt. And then there was a lot of pavement done for the roads. So it took a long time for them to really complete everything. But the parking lot was huge. And by July of '42 the first TNT went off the production line.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. All right. And from what you described this is like a whole community. I mean this is almost self-supporting within the plant itself, within the bounds of the plant.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All the things that are in there. Does anybody stay there? Does anyone live there?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: No, no. There were workers there round the clock all the time. And there was good access to the Tennessee River for their water supply. And when the government -- now I'm going to a different subject here.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: That's fine.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: But the U.S. government, seeing into the future, realized that we would need a lot of powder. And they decided to sponsor the program, pay 100 percent for 50 plants to be established over the United States. And they awarded contracts to construction workers to build all the buildings and facilities and then a contract with the power company, and ours was Hercules. So when I went up there in April of '42, we had this steady line of people coming through for physicals to get them ready to work for Hercules. And a lot of people that were classified as four F applied. Some, of course, were accepted, some could not be. And even soldiers or servicemen wounded in service and having to go to the V.A. for healing, when they were ready to leave the hospital, many of them were not physically able to go back into service and were discharged and then they would come to our plant applying for a job. So I did a lot of x-rays on them, to see in their chest they would still have shrap --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Shrapnel.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: What's that word?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Shrapnel.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Shrapnel in the picture. One man had a heart that was so large it looked like a balloon that would just burst any minute. And there were some funny things about that, too. You saw bad scars. That was not funny. But I had one man up to the x-ray chest board, and he had the wooliest back I have ever seen. And I just wished I had a pair of scissors just to cut a path up through his back there. One case of tuberculosis, it was very, very extensive. When the doctor saw that, they called him in to talk with him about it and we sent him directly to Erlanger Hospital because they had an isolation ward. They didn't even send him home. They took him to the hospital. And I think back on that. Several of us were in contact with this man, like drawing his blood and talking with him. And there I had him in x-ray and was up close with him and nothing was done about any extra cleaning or precautions, although we knew that that was a bad case of tuberculosis.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Excuse me. Now, what is your schedule at this time? Are you working six days a week?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: At work?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Yeah. I know with the swing shift it probably --

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: We worked straight days for quite awhile until the work got so heavy that we had to go on swing shift. We had people come in at staggering times, like seven o'clock, eight a.m., nine a.m. on day shift. And we switched back from swing shift to straight days. When we were on swing shift, it was dull. We would get our work done. We had to see that everything was spic and span clean and plenty of supplies at a moment's notice that we could pick up and use. Everything had to be ready as if an emergency was going to happen. And I don't know who planned the lab and who ordered the first supplies, but they did it in an abundance. We had everything we needed to work with. And we worked Sundays. In fact, everybody worked seven around the clock or I don't remember when we had days off anymore. We did have some time off, of course, but the plant never closed.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: What did you do in your free -- did you have any free time at all? Anything to relax, enjoy yourself?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Oh, when I went home?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Oh, yeah. One thing I did going home was to stop and roll bandages for Red Cross.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Really.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: And we went to movies, roller skating, swimming and of course choir practice.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Did you keep up with what was going on in the war or did that just seem like a long way away?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: I heard my parents and uncle talking more about it. I didn't really read the papers much, but I thought of it a lot. And then we always had somebody that was being called into service. One of our doctors was called to service and this first aid man that I mentioned was called to service. And people were leaving the job. Some just couldn't take it. They could not adjust to the swing shift. And some could not stand the fumes, which were awful. And oh, we had showers. The girls had showers for somebody having a baby or celebration, a birthday celebration or things. We made our own entertainment. It was not a dull life.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right. I was wondering if you were happy during this time.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Happy?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: I was very happy. I enjoyed my work. I enjoyed my rides, talking to the different people and my church work. I was completely -- except for the worry in the back of your mind about your brother being -- mine was in Japan in a hospital. But my friend I was corresponding with, who turned out to be my husband, was in the Air Force, see, and I knew other boys. One fella went into the service, volunteered. And somebody said, any volunteers for the Air Force? Somebody said, why did you do that? He said, I've always wanted to see what was on the other side of the mountain. And he could fly above it. But he was killed in service.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Well, your husband, where did you meet him? Where did you know him from?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: We had known each other always. Our parents were friends, and my parents had a wedding luncheon for his parents when they married. And I have a picture of his mother holding me when I was five months old. So we just always have known each other, although we lived -- he lived at Hairman (ph) and Kingston (ph) and I was at Rossville. We visited each other once a year, and she would come down and bring the boys. I thought that my brother was so good to me and we grew up more or less like twins because our age was so close together. And the others were working and my two sisters became school teachers. And I just thought these boys were so rowdy and they didn't pamper me like my brother did. We played cops and robbers. And if they caught you, and they always caught me and put me in jail, and I had to stay there and I didn't get to play the game.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: So you corresponded with your husband then as --

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: During --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: During the war.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: During the time he was in service. He was drafted and went in at Fort Overthort (ph). And while he was out there, he called our home and talked to us. And from then on I began writing, because they were always saying write to the boys in service. Well, he answered and we just kept a correspondence going.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. Now, and he was flying, right?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And he was flying?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Yes. He went into the Air Force.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. Now, do you remember when Roosevelt died?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Oh, yes. Oh, that's something I wanted to tell you. We had an outdoor PA system. And they played music every day. Whoever was in charge of that music and the records did an excellent job. And when they played something that sort of became a drag or a lull, they would immediately follow it with a peppy song and they played all the patriotic marches. And when Roosevelt died, the flag was half staff for a week and they played religious hymns and classical music for a week. They played hymns every Sunday. And there was one church. Did I tell you about the church?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: On the left-hand side of the main drive going in was a beautiful little white church. And they did not destroy that. And I thought of this scripture let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight. I felt like that whoever was planning in detail had something like that within them, because they saved the church. And it was just a spiritual thing you saw as you could come and go and especially on Sunday. You just looked over and thought that was holy ground. I didn't hear anybody really talking about it, but I'm sure that other people had the same feeling that I did.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: How many people were working there at that time?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Worked there?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Hercules had 2,000 and at one time Stone and Webster had 3,000 plus more later on. See, they were always around. There was things to be done, repaired. I don't know whether they ever left the area.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Tell the story you were just telling me about climbing the steps, having to climb the steps.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Oh, climbing the steps.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Yeah. With the --

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Well, that was difficult. So we could not spill a drop of any of our reagents or the blood that we had that we had diluted. So we asked if we might go to the change house and let the men come to us. And that worked a little better for them not to have to go so far from their working area. But that was not really successful either, and they brought them to the hospital in a station wagon. But that tied up five men for the time that all of them were -- all the work was collected and they could get back on their way, whereas when we went to them, the others were working. We had one at a time. And the foreman of the lines was responsible to see that the men in production had this checkup every six weeks. So we went back to doing all of our collection in the hospital.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right. But talk about the process of having to climb the steps before.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: The --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: You had to climb the steps and there was the spaces between the steps.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Space between the steps. Sometimes we went to the third flight up and then we began stopping at the landing on the second flight and let the people on third, higher up, come down to us. And we got everybody there. Then the people on the second flight could come around to us. We stopped them, then we took our tray and got them from the first floor. And of course someone carried us by station wagon back and forth.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Now, you -- let's see. You say you worked there for 40 months; is that right?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: So -- and you started working there in 19 --

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: April 1942.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: And I left in August of 1945.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. All right. So that's right around VJ day, isn't it?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right around VJ day. Do you remember VE day?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Talk about that.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: There -- we were really excited and very happy about it. But there were a few whose husband had been killed in action. And they were so distressed that the reality that their loved one was not coming home was really hard on them. And we really kind of held back on our celebration there because of them.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right. And is there anything you could do to console or do you try?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Do you do anything to try to console the ones who lost --

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Oh, yes, we did. We talked with them. We had worked with them for a long time.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. Now, is there any thought in your mind that maybe your future husband will end up being your husband at this time or --

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: No, no. It's just that we were friends, knew each other so well. And he went on his way. And after the war, after I left the TNT plant, I went back to college and got the requirements to take the national registration exam for medical technologist. And then later Tennessee came up with a licensure, and I took that exam and was licensed as a hematologist specialist for -- in Tennessee. And I actually worked 29 years for Erlanger and three and a half at the TNT plant and public health part-time job while I was in college. So I worked about 37 years as a med tech.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Well, when did you end up -- how did you end up getting together with your husband and eventually marrying him?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Getting together with him?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Well, he came home. And when he came home from Okinawa, it was a surprise to his family and me.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Had he stayed over there in occupation thing?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Um-hum, for two years. And since we were such close friends and I was working late for two nights a week, 8:30 -- eight o'clock one night, 8:30 one night. And it was a bitter cold night, and his mother knew that I had trouble then of getting home. My communication was not as good then as it was when I was working at the TNT plant. So she called me and she said, oh, it's such a bad night tonight. Why don't you come and spend the night at our house. And so I caught the bus and went a short distance down to their house. But while she was talking to me -- I did go down to their house. While she was talking to me, she said, oh, here's T. And that's his nickname. And he came in, coming home from Okinawa, and found out what our conversation was about and says, tell her I'll come and pick her up. Because he bought a car after he came in to Chattanooga that afternoon before he came home. And he came and picked me up and from then on we began dating.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: How long did it end up -- how long before you ended up getting married? He went back to Okinawa.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Well, we dated a year, and he went back to Okinawa for five months and came home and we married in June of 1950.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. We have to stop for a second.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: During my tenure there I worked for 10 different doctors. There were at least nine nurses, seven med techs, several of the first aid men, safety engineer was around our hospital all the time, four ambulance drivers, file clerks and receptionists, one maid. She had a college graduate -- a college degree.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: The maid?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Actually, she was the only black help we had in the way of a maid. I don't think I told you something about the site. After the government decided to build these plants, Senator Kiefoffer (ph) and Ed Bass, the mayor of Chattanooga, and other officials worked real hard to get this into Chattanooga. So this site was selected, and they had -- did I tell you a thousand -- 8,058 acres.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: And am I losing time here?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: No, no. We have about another minute and another tape. CAROLYN: The cost of the project.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: This is going back to my work. Did I tell you about the man that had the infection?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: There was a fellow who had been to Tullahoma and there was war work over there. And he had an infection from it in his arm from the venous culture. He sued the plant and won 50,000 dollars. That healed. He came to Hercules and applied for a job, and I collected his blood. [Tape is changed.]

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Let's go back. So he comes back in and applies and you draw his blood.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: And I draw his blood. A little later, a few days later I was called into the medical director's office. There was a man sitting there, well dressed and nice looking fella. He was an attorney for Hercules Company and I thought, oh, what have I done? And this fella that had the infection at Tullahoma was the one that I _______ and his arm was giving the same reaction. It peeled skin off in layers, was really bad. Of course there was some time lapse between the two, but he was suing Hercules. And this attorney must have done some really good research work. He did not win his case with Hercules. And we had an order from our director not to collect blood from any person with that last name, because they decided that the problem was an allergy to the metal of the needle. I never heard it before and haven't heard it since, but that's what they figured out. And he had a bad looking arm. I had to tell the attorney my whole procedure for collecting a specimen.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Now, let's talk about -- you wanted to mention the cost of the project.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Well, headlines in the paper in Chattanooga on June the sixth, 1941, city to get 39 million dollars for munition plant. And then it told about who was working for it to try to get the site and then another time the paper said 23,000 -- did she say a million or a thousand for road paving within the site?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: So everything was well taken care of and clean and well kept.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. Now --

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Not many funny things happened. I mean we enjoyed our work and laughed and talked. But we had another medical director. Dr. Whitley left and this doctor came in, Dr. Preston. And I was working in x-ray. He began sending people down there with his orders written on a tongue depressor. It's really cute. GI series or chest x-ray, whatever you wanted was written in ink on tongue depressors rather than on a requisition. Of course I did the work. And while I was working there, our x-ray table was flat with a rolling carrier that held the tube, so you could place the tube anywhere you wanted or turn it up for the chest board. And getting ready to go home, I was trying to get the carrier back in a position I left it every afternoon and the rollers caught the cord and -- oh, this fell off. [Ms. Mahoney's microphone fell off.]

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: All right. I was in there alone trying to pull the cord out from under the rollers, and I got this carrier off balance and it fell over me onto the floor. And the tube hit the floor so hard that it chipped that hard floor. I was scared to death. I rushed in. I didn't know whether there were rays escaping or not. I rushed in and pulled the switch and then went down to tell Dr. Preston. And the tube had to be sent for repair. It was an expensive repair job. But I thought he was real cute the way he sent his orders on those little strips of wood.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Other funny stories? Anything funny you can think of or any stories that happened at the plant?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Any other interesting stories or funny stories while you were at the plant you want to bring up?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: I guess I've left out something. I can tell you about the Christmas party when I got the cologne.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: We had a little Christmas party and I was given a bottle of cologne. And I couldn't wait to get home to open it and see how good it smelled, but the top was hard to remove. So I cracked it on the top of a table and just broke the top straight across on that bottle, but my thumb would fit over the hole. So I rode on the outside of -- to the outside so I could hold my hand outside the window as we drove home and that stuff was slosh, slosh. By the time I got home, I was so sick of smelling that it gave me a headache and I threw the gift away. CAROLYN: Did you tell him about the gift that you got from the TNT plant when it opened; when the first round went through?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: I didn't understand you, Carolyn.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: The gift you got from the TNT plant when the first round came through.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Oh, the vial of TNT from the first --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Oh, really.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: -- production.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Talk about it.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Oh, they gave each employee a small glass vial with a cap on it as a souvenir, because you could carry it and it was not dangerous. But when I got home with it and showed it to my family, my mother said, get this stuff out of the house. So I took it out and tossed it out on the hillside.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Oh, really. You didn't keep it?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: No, I didn't keep it. I wish I had. But it was an interesting place to work and very rewarding I felt. And it was always interesting when the four F people came. It was interesting to talk with them. They didn't mind talking about their experience. And I didn't tell you where our doctors were from, did I? One doctor was from New York, one from New Jersey, who was drafted or called into service after he got there, one from Florida, two Seventh Day Adventists, one who gave up a job at a TB sanitarium to come and work at our place, and one -- two who were retired general practitioners. And they came back into service and worked up there until peace was declared. When we were dismissed they gave us one month's pay as severance pay. What they owed us plus one month's pay. And did I ever tell you my salary?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: No, you didn't.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Well, I was delighted. We made 300 a month, and that was a great jump from 15 cents an hour.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right. How long did you end up at Erlanger or how long did you end up working afterward? You mentioned it once.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Twenty-nine years.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Twenty-nine. That's very impressive. All right.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: I taught students and enjoyed the students. They brought in new life to the place. It kept you from getting a little bit bored maybe if you were doing the same thing over and over and over. But on our job at Erlanger -- I mean at the plant we rotated. And our supervisor was very conscientious of time. She didn't want any wasted time. We had the newest edition of textbooks on the counter or shelf that we could look up anything we needed to, but she didn't want us to read that and discuss it with each other. That looked like you were wasting time. And defrosting our refrigerator, she had that done over and over. If somebody called up -- like she'd say, Miss Au, go defrost the refrigerator. Well, great, it had been defrosted about three days before. And then the slides were packed 140 -- ________ slides for blood smears were packed 144 to a pack. They felt gritty and needed to be rinsed through alcohol and dried and then repacked for us to make good smears. And we had boxes and boxes washed and ready. So got through and there's still a little bit of time before you go home, you went to wash more slides. You emptied those boxes of clean slides and started over. She kept us busy all the time.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Makes the time pass faster though, doesn't it?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Makes the time pass faster though, doesn't it?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Yes, it did. And it kept us from getting into trouble, I guess.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Did you feel like -- while you were here that you were really contributing to the war effort? Was that ever on your mind or was it just a really --

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: A job?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: The only thing that made me feel like it was for the war effort was the fact that we were making something needed for ammunition.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: And that was always uppermost in our minds I think.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: We wanted to do our job well. But those men worked hard and it was not good for their health. We did a lot of gastric analysis and as I said GIs, the fluoroscopes, a test that could be due to stress or brought a tumor, ulcers. Oh, I have to tell you something funny about that. One hospital member -- not hospital. A member of the administration was a very, very cocky fella. I'm sure he was intelligent and understood his job, but he made many trips to the hospital and come down on his lunch break, coming from the administration building to our hospital, and he would go in one of these rooms with a single bed and close the door. He went in there to sleep. And I don't know that a doctor had told him he could do that or should do that. But we had cards that were printed up to hand out to employees, war worker sleeping. That was to put on their door at home when they were going home to sleep from the night shift. So we put that on his door one day and when he came out he saw it and he yanked it down. Well, he came back again. And we had to work with interval timers. Many, many things that we did were timed, five minutes, 10 minutes, whatever. And these were wind-up clocks. So we gathered our clocks and put 'em on a shelf on the wall that was next to his room. And we had those going off 15 minutes, 10 minutes, five minutes. We just kept clocks ringing. And he got up and came out of there and never came back.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: We have about eight minutes left. Is there anything you can think of that you want to bring up?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: I still have more time?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Well, I mean we don't have to fill it.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Oh, Carolyn, do you recall how much you said that the pavement cost? Was it 23 million or 23,000? CAROLYN: The whole company --

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Was 39,000. CAROLYN: -- was 39 million and the roads were 323,000.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Twenty-three thousand. Well, they worked hard. They did a good job up there. And as you know or have heard, there was TNT in storage and it has been used for the other wars, Korea, Vietnam. And it was opened again for Vietnam by another company.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right. All right. Anything you want to mention? Anything else that you can think of that we left out? It looks like we pretty much covered everything.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Well, we had a dietitian. The two cafeterias had good food and we had a dietitian that was very active, busy. Oh, I'll tell you about getting to work and transportation. I rode with one of our receptionists who lived a few miles from where I walked from home to Rossville two miles and waited at the post office for a lot of my rides. I was riding with her. She drove up and she said, oh, I'm drunk. And I thought I've got to go to work and I didn't know whether to get in the car with her or not and I could not drive. But I did. I rode on to work with her. Well, another morning her husband drove up. He was an officer at Fort Overthort. He said, my wife said to pick you up and take you over to Ringo Road at McBryan (ph), and you can stand there and get a ride to the plant. Well, it was one of the main thoroughfares. I did that. I got out and stood there until somebody recognized me and picked me up. And I got to work on time. Oh, there's one more thing I wanted to say. I don't remember what it was. So I guess that's it.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Hold on one second.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: That will make something -- freeze something. What do you call that, Carolyn? In a can and it was a spray. CAROLYN: Aerosol?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: What? CAROLYN: Aerosol?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: No. It was a chemical name. You could deaden things, deaden the area around a cut or something. You could treat poison ivy. CAROLYN: Novocain?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: No. But it was something that would freeze. One night when we didn't have much to do -- our 11 to seven shifts were very, very dull. I'd think of somebody I would want to talk to, but I'd look at the clock and it was no time to make a telephone call. We were all in the treatment room and double doors were open and a little mouse ran in. One of the boys grabbed up this spray can and he began squirting it and it froze that little rat. It was as white as snow with eyes. And I never did see any more rats in there either.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Pretty smart creatures. Anything else you can think of?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Oh, how I got my telephone.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: That was important. We were on call. I think I told you that. We were all on call and we didn't have a phone. And it was very difficult to get a telephone at that time. So they sent papers from the plant to South Bell I guess it was then to explain the need for a telephone. And in just a few days a phone was put in at our home, two-party line, and the bill was eight dollars and 49 cents a month.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: I'd rather not have a phone.

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: In case they wanted to call me, you're without a phone. Anything else you can think of?

sp.speaker: Dora Janet Au Mahoney
sp.p: I think that's the rest of my stories.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. I thank you for your time.
